question: What does Starlette.build_middleware_stack() do, and in what order are the middleware layers applied to an incoming request?
What does ServerErrorMiddleware do when the app it wraps raises an exception, and how does its behaviour differ between debug=True and debug=False?
What is ExceptionMiddleware responsible for, and which exceptions does it handle by default?
What does Route.matches(scope) return, and what specifically does a Match.PARTIAL result indicate?
What does Request.stream() do, and how does it prevent the request body from being consumed twice?
How does Request.body() behave differently from Request.stream() when called more than once?
What does BackgroundTasks.__call__ do, and how are synchronous vs asynchronous task functions executed?
What HTTP status code does RedirectResponse use by default, and why does that particular choice matter?
When Config is given both an environment variable and an entry in the .env file for the same key, which value wins, and how does Config.__call__ resolve it?
Trace, across files, how an unhandled ValueError raised inside an HTTP endpoint becomes a 500 response.
How do ExceptionMiddleware and routing.py cooperate to turn a raised HTTPException into an HTTP response?
How does Mount interact with Router so that a mounted sub-application only sees its own sub-path?
How does Starlette.add_middleware relate to build_middleware_stack, and why does calling add_middleware after the application has started serving raise a RuntimeError?
How does a class-based HTTPEndpoint end up being invoked by a Route?
How does request.state relate to state yielded by a lifespan context and to scope['state']?
How does TestClient run the ASGI app, and at what point is the application lifespan actually executed?
How does CORSMiddleware short-circuit a CORS preflight request before the routing layer runs?
What are the major components of Starlette, and how are they layered when handling an HTTP request?
Describe the primary data flow from the ASGI scope/receive/send triple to an endpoint and back to the client.
Where are Starlette's system boundaries? Specifically, what does it delegate to the ASGI server and what does it delegate to anyio?
The middleware stack and the routing tree are two different mechanisms. What is each responsible for, and why are they not the same thing?
How does the WebSocket request path diverge from the HTTP path while going through the same application stack?
Which three or four files should a new maintainer read first to understand Starlette, and why those?

Suppose Request.__init__ were changed to require a non-empty, always-callable receive channel (today it defaults receive to a stub that is only valid if the body is never read). What in the codebase would break or need updating?
If ServerErrorMiddleware stopped re-raising the exception after sending the 500 response, what downstream behaviour would change?
What in routing.py depends on Match being an ordered enum where FULL > PARTIAL > NONE?
If BackgroundTasks were changed to run its tasks concurrently (e.g. in an anyio task group) instead of sequentially, what could break in existing applications?
What is the blast radius of changing JSONResponse's default separators (currently compact ',' ':') or its media_type?
If build_middleware_stack were changed so ExceptionMiddleware wrapped the OUTSIDE of user middleware (instead of the inside), what would change for application authors?

An endpoint raises HTTPException(status_code=404). Separately, a plain-ASGI user middleware above routing raises HTTPException(status_code=400) on some requests. Which case yields a clean 4xx response and which yields a 500, and why?
A request's path matches a route registered with methods=['GET'], but the request method is DELETE. What status code and what headers are returned, and through which code path?
A client requests GET /items but the only route is /items/ (with a trailing slash). With default settings, what does the client get? What changes if the Router is created with redirect_slashes=False?
An endpoint returns a Response with three BackgroundTasks attached. The second task raises an exception. What does the client see, and do the first and third tasks run?
Inside one endpoint, the code does `await request.json()` and then later `await request.body()`. Does the second call fail? Separately, what happens if the code iterates `request.stream()` twice?

A contextvar.ContextVar is set inside a BaseHTTPMiddleware.dispatch() implementation (after calling call_next). Is that value visible to code running outside/above that middleware, or to a later request? Why?
GZipMiddleware is installed with defaults. A handler returns a 120-byte JSON body and the request has 'Accept-Encoding: gzip'. Is the response compressed?

CORSMiddleware is configured with allow_origins=['*'] and allow_credentials=True. A browser sends a credentialed cross-origin request from https://app.example.com. What Access-Control-Allow-Origin header does Starlette send, and can the browser use the response?

An app is defined with a lifespan async context manager that raises RuntimeError during startup (before its yield). What happens when the app is served by an ASGI server, and what happens under TestClient?

docs/middleware.md presents the execution order as 'ServerErrorMiddleware -> [user middleware] -> ExceptionMiddleware -> Routing -> Endpoint'. Does build_middleware_stack implement exactly that, and is there anything the docs omit?

Do the Starlette docs anywhere explicitly warn that an exception raised inside a middleware bypasses ExceptionMiddleware and the registered exception handlers? Does the implementation behave that way regardless of whether the docs warn?
Compare docs/background.md with background.py: is the documented behaviour (tasks run after the response; error handling) fully accurate?
Does docs/requests.md accurately describe Request.body()/stream() caching, or is there a mismatch or omission?

docs/middleware.md has a 'BaseHTTPMiddleware - Limitations' section stating contextvar changes don't propagate upward. Is that the only practically-relevant limitation, judged against middleware/base.py?
What evidence in the repository supports the claim 'ServerErrorMiddleware is always the outermost middleware layer'? Cite source, docs, and tests.
What evidence supports the claim 'a partial route match (path matches, method does not) produces a 405 with an Allow header'? Cite source and tests.
What evidence supports 'background tasks run after the response body is sent'? Cite source and tests.
What evidence supports 'TestClient runs the application lifespan only when it is used as a context manager'? Cite source and tests.

Assess this developer's explanation for correctness, and correct any misconception: 'If I register @app.exception_handler(HTTPException), it will catch any HTTPException raised anywhere in my app, including ones I raise from my own custom middleware.'

Assess for correctness and correct any misconception: 'Background tasks are a good place to decide whether to send the user a different response -- e.g. if the task fails, return a 500 to the client instead.'
Assess for correctness and correct any misconception: 'redirect_slashes sends a 301 so the browser caches the corrected URL and future requests skip the redirect.'

Assess for correctness and correct any misconception: 'When I Mount a sub-application at /v1, the routes inside that sub-application have to be declared with the /v1 prefix, like Route("/v1/users", ...).'

Novel scenario: 'In production, one of my endpoints sees a request header that a middleware of mine is supposed to have deleted. Reason about where a header deletion can and cannot take effect in Starlette, and where I should look.'
Novel scenario: 'We want unhandled 500s to return a JSON error body for API clients instead of the default plain text. Where do we hook in Starlette, and what must we be careful about?'

Novel scenario: 'Under load, a small fraction of responses are missing a custom header that our BaseHTTPMiddleware adds after call_next. Generate plausible hypotheses grounded in how Starlette works.'

Novel scenario: 'We deployed our app behind a proxy that serves it under /api, and we mount a sub-app at /v2 inside it. request.url_for() in the sub-app now produces URLs missing the /api prefix. Reason about root_path.'
